Well, doctor, if you want the honest truth, it’s my wife who made the appointment. What brings me in is... well, it’s this memorial I’m putting together for my brother. I just wanted to do something small at first, you know, just a respectful little gathering to honor him. But... well, it’s just gotten bigger than I ever meant it to. Much, much bigger. 

I mean, there's just so much that goes into it if you want to do it right. I’ve been spending most days—really, from the minute I wake up until late into the night—just chasing down things for it. But as for *having* to do it... yes, I suppose it feels like a compulsion, in a way. Like a... a duty. A sacred duty, almost. If I don't do it, who will? My sister? She barely even visits. And once I started making the list of people to contact, it just kept growing. First it was just family, then close friends, then I remembered his old bowling league—the one from the 80s, you know, over at the lanes that closed down—and I realized I had to track all those guys down. And then the ideas for the displays started coming to me. It’s like the ideas just pop into my head, one after the other, bang, bang, bang, and I have to write them down and I have to execute them. 

I wake up at, oh, maybe 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, and my mind is just racing with all the things I need to get done for it. The catering, the invitations, the speech... oh, the speech! I've rewritten it probably fifteen times. I just can't seem to stop until everything is absolutely perfect. So, yes, I want to do it, but I also feel like I can't *not* do it, if you understand what I'm saying. It's just... it's all I can think about.

It’s a lot of work, a whole lot of moving parts, and I just have to keep on top of it all. \n\nBut my wife, she’s just about had it with me. She says I’m overdoing it. She keeps telling me I’ve completely pushed aside the spring garden—and sure, the weeds are getting a little high out back, I know that—and she's upset I stopped going to my morning walking group. She says I’ve pushed aside just about everything else in my life for this memorial. But how can I stop when there are still so many people to call and arrangements to make? Anyway, she said I had to come talk to you about it, so here I am.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have to do all these things for the memorial, or is it more that you want to do them?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... it’s a bit of both, honestly. I mean, I *want* to do it, of course I do. He was my brother. We were two years apart, practically attached at the hip growing up. We used to sneak out and listen to the radio in his old Chevy—that’s why the music is so important, you see. I have to get the music right. If I don't get the exact version of \"Born to Run\" that we listened to on 8-track in the summer of '74, the whole feeling of the memorial is just going to be off. \n\nBut as for *having* to do it... yes, I suppose it feels like a compulsion, in a way. And then the ideas for the displays started coming to me. It’s like the ideas just pop into my head, one after the other, bang, bang, bang, and I have to write them down and I have to execute them. \n\nI wake up at, oh, maybe 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, and my mind is just racing with all the things I need to get done for it. And the garden... well, I know I said the weeds are getting a little high, but honestly, it's worse than that. I usually have the tomatoes and the bell peppers in by now, the soil all tilled and perfectly fertilized, but it’s just sitting there going to seed. \n\nBut it’s the people, really, that seem to be the biggest issue lately. I go down to the senior center, right? And I try to talk to my friends there about the displays, because I’m building these massive, beautiful, chronological display boards of his life, and I just needed to explain the vision to them. I thought maybe I could use a few tables in the rec room to lay out the foam core and the photos to get it all organized. But they got so... so dismissive! I guess I got pretty irritated with them, and maybe I raised my voice a bit, because they just didn't get the scale of what I'm doing. Now a bunch of folks there are all upset with me, saying everything I talk about is the memorial display and I don't care about anything else. She says she’s constantly having to talk me out of taking another spontaneous road trip to track someone down, or pulling me away from an argument with the printer over the exact weight of the invitation cardstock. Distress? Well... no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, what exactly do you mean by distress? If you mean, am I sitting around crying or wringing my hands over the planning, then absolutely not. Honestly, it’s the exact opposite. I feel... well, I feel like I finally have a real purpose again. You know, since I retired from the plant—which was a whole ordeal in itself, let me tell you, thirty-five years there and they barely gave me a proper send-off—but since then, I haven't had a project that really required my full attention. And this? This is vital.

So, no, the efforts aren't causing me distress. I mean, sure, I'm busy. I'm incredibly busy. Just last night, I was up at, oh, it must have been 2:30 or 3:00 in the morning, because I suddenly realized that the font on the invitations was all wrong. The printer wanted to use some standard, modern lettering, but my brother was a traditionalist, you see. So I spent hours, literally hours, going through these typography samples online, comparing all these different styles, because the little tails on the letters, they have to look dignified, don't they? And doing that, finding the exact right detail... it doesn't distress me. It’s exhilarating! I feel sharper than I have in years, like all the cylinders are finally firing at once. 

If anything is causing me distress, it’s just... it’s the people who don't understand the vision. It's Martha constantly hovering over my shoulder, sighing heavily every time I pick up the telephone to make a simple inquiry. Or that kid at the print shop, he had the nerve to tell me my timeline was unrealistic. Unrealistic! I told him flat out that I am the customer, and if I need two hundred custom-embossed programs by Tuesday, he needs to figure it out. So, it’s the friction with everyone else that's frustrating. The actual work of planning the memorial? No, not distressing in the slightest. It's just a matter of getting everyone else to step back and let me do what needs to be done.

Well, let's see... it’s been about two months now. Yes, right around two months. It started pretty much the exact day he passed, to be honest with you. Work? Oh, well, no. No, I haven't had any problems with a job because... well, like I mentioned a little while ago, I'm retired. I put in thirty-five years at the manufacturing plant. Thirty-five years! And let me tell you, if I were still working there, I don't know how I'd ever manage everything I'm doing right now. Brought in all these kids straight out of school who barely know how to hold a clipboard, gave me a cheap grocery store sheet cake and a handshake, and sent me on my way. It still leaves a bad taste in my mouth, to be honest with you. Which, if you think about it, is exactly why this memorial has to be perfect. You can't just slap something together and call it a tribute, like the plant did with my retirement! People deserve to have their lives honored properly. You have to put in the effort, the real detail work. 

So, to answer your question, no, I haven't lost a job over this. Planning this memorial is my job right now. It's a full-time job, more than a full-time job, really. It's the most important work I've ever done, and frankly, it requires a lot more vision and dedication than they ever let me use at the plant anyway. If anything, not having a job is the only reason I can finally give this project the respect it demands.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Lost friends? Well, lost is a very strong word, isn't it? I mean, they're not dead, like my brother, they're just... they're just being incredibly petty about the whole thing. People have such a limited capacity to understand true dedication, I'm finding. 

Take my walking group, for instance. I've been walking with Frank and Arthur around the reservoir every Tuesday and Thursday for, oh, it must be five years now. And just because I've missed a few weeks—well, maybe a month and a half of walks—they're acting like I've committed some sort of crime! I tried to explain to Arthur on the telephone that I can't just go strolling around looking at ducks when I have to finalize the seating charts and track down a specific type of ivory cardstock, but he just gave me this heavy sigh. I haven't been to my book club either, because honestly, who has time to sit around reading made-up stories when you are trying to cement a man's actual, factual legacy? I've even let the garden go completely. The tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine as we speak, but you have to prioritize, you see. You have to make sacrifices for greatness.

But the real issue, the thing that really caused a stink, was down at the senior center. I went down there last week to set up a preliminary memorial display—just a small one, a trifold board with some photographs, a few personal artifacts, some drapery, just to get people's feedback on the aesthetic before the main event. And you would not believe the fuss they made! A couple of the guys I usually play pinochle with got incredibly upset, telling me I was taking up the whole recreation room and that I was being obsessive. Obsessive! Can you believe that? Just because everything I talk about right now is the memorial display. Well, what else is there to talk about? My brother's life is a masterpiece waiting to be curated, and they want to talk about their golf handicaps. It's insulting. 

And Martha... well, my wife is just being impossible about the whole situation. She actually sat me down and had the nerve to say that our entire days revolve around her trying to calm me down. Calm me down! I am perfectly calm, I am just energized! She says she's constantly having to redirect me, like I'm a child, trying to stop me from making another phone call to the caterer, or taking another trip down to the venue to check the lighting, or getting into an argument with someone who doesn't understand the timeline. She thinks I'm the one causing the friction! 

So, have I lost friends? I suppose if you look at it from the outside, maybe I'm not socializing the way I used to. But frankly, if they can't support me and recognize the absolute necessity of what I'm doing right now, then I simply don't have the time or the patience for them anyway.

It’s like the ideas just pop into my head, one after the other, bang, bang, bang, and I have to write them down and I have to execute them. \n\nI wake up at, oh, maybe 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, and my mind is just racing with all the things I need to get done for it. The catering, the invitations, the speech... oh, the speech! I've rewritten it probably fifteen times. I just can't seem to stop until everything is absolutely perfect. So, yes, I want to do it, but I also feel like I can't *not* do it, if you understand what I'm saying. We were supposed to be reading this fascinating historical biography, but I couldn't even tell you where my copy of the book is right now because my desk and the entire dining room table are just covered, absolutely covered, in memorial plans and guest lists. And the garden... well, I know I said the weeds are getting a little high, but honestly, it's worse than that. I thought maybe I could use a few tables in the rec room to lay out the foam core and the photos to get it all organized. But they got so... so dismissive! I guess I got pretty irritated with them, and maybe I raised my voice a bit, because they just didn't get the scale of what I'm doing. She tells me her entire day revolves around trying to calm me down, or physically redirecting me away from the telephone so I don't make another call to a caterer or a distant cousin at dinnertime. She says she’s constantly having to talk me out of taking another spontaneous road trip to track someone down, or pulling me away from an argument with the printer over the exact weight of the invitation cardstock. She thinks I'm just looking for a fight, but I'm just trying to get it right! It’s just... there’s so much to do, and if everyone would just let me work on it and see the vision instead of getting in my way, we wouldn't be having these problems.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your efforts to plan the memorial are causing you significant emotional distress?\n\nPatient: Distress? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Justified? Well... I suppose that really depends entirely on how you look at the situation, doesn't it? Because from where she's standing, I'm sure it looks like I'm just being difficult. But she doesn't see the vision. She doesn't feel what I'm feeling right now. 

I mean, I will wake up in the morning, or even in the middle of the night, and I just feel completely lit up inside. It's this incredible sensation, like I am just full to the brim with purpose. I’ll be standing there in the dining room, looking over the blueprints for the seating arrangements or the drapery swatches, and I get this overwhelming sense that the whole town is finally going to understand our family. They're finally going to see what my brother meant to this community, what we are all about. It’s a glorious feeling, really. It’s like a warm fire in my chest, pushing me forward, telling me that this is exactly what I was put on this earth to do. 

But then... well, yes, I suppose the flip side of that is I do get a bit short with people. More than a bit short, if I'm being perfectly honest. One minute I am riding high on this wave of inspiration, and the next minute, I snap. I just completely snap at her. Or at those guys down at the senior center. Because they come in, and they try to slow me down! Martha will come up behind me and put her hand on my shoulder and tell me I need to stop calling the florist, or one of the pinochle guys will start questioning why the trifold display needs to take up three tables, and it just infuriates me! 

How can they not see it? When you have this much drive, this much energy pushing you toward a masterpiece, having someone try to pull the emergency brake on you is agonizing. So, yes, I bite their heads off. I yell. I tell them to get out of my way. If they would just stop questioning the display, if they would just stop trying to slow my progress and let me work, I wouldn't have to snap at them! So I don't know if her complaints are "justified," doctor. I suppose nobody likes being yelled at, but if you ask me, if she would just get on board and help me instead of acting like a roadblock, we wouldn't be having this problem in the first place.

Because, you see, the funeral home did their standard little service right after, and I was sitting there in the second pew, looking at this incredibly generic, cheap floral arrangement they’d put together, and I just knew—I knew right then and there—that it wasn't enough for him. It's a full-time job, more than a full-time job, really. I suppose I have let a whole lot of my normal life slide right off the table, and people are definitely holding a grudge about it. And Martha... well, my wife is just at her wit's end, I suppose. I'll be picking up the phone to make just one more necessary call to the caterer, or grabbing my car keys to take one more trip down to the venue just to measure the entryway for the floral arches, or I'm getting into a perfectly justified argument with the venue manager because they don't understand the timeline, and there's Martha, always pulling at my sleeve, trying to stop me and redirect my attention.

Every single day since he passed. I’ll be standing there in the dining room, looking over the blueprints for the seating arrangements or the drapery swatches, and I get this overwhelming sense that the whole town is finally going to understand our family. They're finally going to see what my brother meant to this community, what we are all about. It’s a glorious feeling, really. It’s like a warm fire in my chest, pushing me forward, telling me that this is exactly what I was put on this earth to do. \n\nBut then... well, yes, I suppose the flip side of that is I do get a bit short with people. More than a bit short, if I'm being perfectly honest. One minute I am riding high on this wave of inspiration, and the next minute, I snap. I just completely snap at her. Or at those guys down at the senior center. Because they come in, and they try to slow me down! Martha will come up behind me and put her hand on my shoulder and tell me I need to stop calling the florist, or one of the pinochle guys will start questioning why the trifold display needs to take up three tables, and it just infuriates me! \n\nHow can they not see it? When you have this much drive, this much energy pushing you toward a masterpiece, having someone try to pull the emergency brake on you is agonizing. So, yes, I bite their heads off. I yell. I tell them to get out of my way. If they would just stop questioning the display, if they would just stop trying to slow my progress and let me work, I wouldn't have to snap at them! So I don't know if her complaints are \"justified,\" doctor. I suppose nobody likes being yelled at, but if you ask me, if she would just get on board and help me instead of acting like a roadblock, we wouldn't be having this problem in the first place.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your relationships with friends and family have been damaged beyond repair because of your focus on the memorial?\n\nPatient: Damaged beyond repair? Well, I certainly hope not. I mean, people cool off eventually, don't they? Time heals all wounds, as they say. But... I suppose I have let a whole lot of my normal life slide right off the table, and people are definitely holding a grudge about it. Like I was telling you before about Frank and Arthur and the walking group—I haven't been in weeks. And my book club! We were supposed to be reading this historical biography, a really thick one about Roosevelt, which usually I love, you know, reading about the great men of history and how they built their legacies. But I haven't shown my face there in over a month. I haven't even looked at my garden out back. The weeds are probably knee-high by the tomatoes, just completely let the whole yard go to seed. But I had to! Because every single waking moment, every single conversation I have, everything has become entirely about the memorial display. I'll be picking up the phone to make just one more necessary call to the caterer, or grabbing my car keys to take one more trip down to the venue just to measure the entryway for the floral arches, or I'm getting into a perfectly justified argument with the venue manager because they don't understand the timeline, and there's Martha, always pulling at my sleeve, trying to stop me and redirect my attention. \n\nSo, beyond repair? I don't know. Once they see the final memorial, once they walk in and see the absolute perfection of it, I think they'll understand why I had to miss the walks and the books and the gardening. Have to or want to? Well, doctor, that’s a... that’s a very interesting way to put it. You see, it started out as something I just wanted to do. It’s for my brother, you know. I don't think I actually mentioned that yet—it's my brother's memorial. And I just wanted to do something nice, something respectable for him.

So now, do I feel like I *have* to do it? It feels like an absolute duty, a calling! I just can't stop. I’ve been spending most of my days, from the crack of dawn until late into the night, just chasing down the perfect songs. And then there's the phone calls. I'm calling folks all over the country—distant cousins in Ohio, his old army buddies, people who haven't even seen him in twenty years—coordinating travel, making sure they have the itinerary. And I'm planning all these elaborate displays, putting together shadow boxes of his medals, mapping out trips back and forth to the venue to make sure the sightlines are right for the projector... it just snowballed. It completely snowballed on me. 

And like I was telling you before about Martha, she’s the one who finally put her foot down. She says I’ve pushed aside the garden, the walking group with Frank and Arthur, and just about everything else in my normal life just to chase down all these details. But when you're in the thick of it, when you're planning displays and making a hundred calls for your own brother... you don't even realize how massive the whole production has gotten until it's the only thing you're doing.
